item.title: Agent Identity and Authority: A Research Framework for Evaluating Enforceable Security Boundaries in Autonomous AI Systems
item.description: The Agent Identity and Authority Lab (AIAL) is an independent cybersecurity research initiative examining the effectiveness of enforceable identity, delegated authority, and authorization controls for autonomous AI agents. This pre-experimental research proposal establishes a framework for evaluating the distinction between behavioral guardrails and independently enforced security boundaries. item.title: Persistent Semantic Agency: An Architecture for Agent Systems Beyond the Loop
item.description: Persistent Semantic Agency argues that the architectural center of an intelligent agent system must move from the trajectory of a model to a persistent semantic system of delegated commitments, structured work, knowledge, memory, responsibility, authority, and evidence. item.title: An evaluation guided multiagent framework for generating floor plans that comply with municipal building regulations
item.description: Abstract Generative models often produce perceptually plausible outputs that violate hard domain rules. In architectural layout generation, balancing geometric intuition with regulatory compliance remains a persistent challenge, as current frameworks routinely fail to conform to local building laws. item.description: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly deployed at the edge to support complex tasks that require collaboration and information exchange among multiple agents. item.description: ABSTRACT Objective Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming artificial intelligence applications, but their unprecedented computational, memory, communication, and data‐management demands pose significant challenges to existing computing infrastructures. item.title: MemScope: Evolving Agent Memory Architectures through Localized Code Repair
item.description: Agent memory architectures define how LLM agents store and reuse experience across tasks, but they are typically fixed after deployment, limiting their adaptability across task types. Recent self-evolving approaches instead adapt these memory architectures using execution feedback, typically represented as evaluation scores or compressed summaries. item.title: Learning to Steer LLM Agents and Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: Large language model (LLM)-based agents and multi-agent systems increasingly tackle complex tasks through long-horizon tool use and inter-agent collaboration. However, these systems are prone to deviating from the overall goal as execution unfolds, which wastes execution resources and leads to undesired outcomes, a failure termed goal drift. item.description: Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. item.title: Auditing Escalation Reliability in Healthcare LLM Agents: A Perturbation-Controlled Benchmark of Workflow-State Failures

item.title: OS-Helix: Unifying GUI Interaction and Code Execution in Native Computer-Using Agents
item.description: Real desktop automation is neither purely visual nor purely programmatic. Agents must understand user-facing interfaces while efficiently manipulating files, scripts, and system state. However, native GUI/code coordination cannot be obtained by prompt-level tool composition. item.title: From utterances to actionable labels: Toward practical and scalable open intent discovery in production systems
item.description: This thesis presents novel contributions to the field of Open Intent Discovery (OID), addressing fundamental challenges in the unsupervised identification and labelling of user intents within unlabelled datasets. Existing work in OID often relies on small, static, and clean datasets, lacks robust methods for generating interpretable intent labels, and exhibits inconsistencies in evaluation methodologies. item.title: Beyond Task Delegation: Reconceptualising Instructional Design to Measure Competence in the Age of Generative AI
item.description: The rapid proliferation of Large Language Models (LLMs) has invalidated traditional content-recall assessments, acting as a catalyst for a systemic transition towards Competence-Based Education (CBE). This paper contends that the role of faculty must transcend content dissemination, focusing instead on observable human competencies associated with Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning (SRL). item.description: Abstract SIRS 2026, held under the theme “Schizophrenia Research in the Era of Artificial Intelligence,” brought together researchers, clinicians, and persons with lived experience to take stock of a field whose tools for measuring, predicting, and intervening in psychosis have expanded rapidly. item.title: Fragmented control, collective risk: multi‐agent AI and the coming governance crisis
item.description: Abstract Multi‐agent artificial intelligence (MAAI) systems are increasingly deployed across economic and digital infrastructures. Existing regulatory frameworks, including the EU AI Act and related initiatives, largely focus on individual AI systems and are therefore poorly suited to govern risks that arise from agent interaction.
